questions.a: It depends on how they are planted. SWE-smith's difficulty model (1 easy, 5 medium, 9 hard) rated model-modified bugs 3.3 and random-edit bugs 3.6 on average, against 5.01 for full SWE-bench and 3.96 for SWE-bench Verified; rewritten functions (5.27) and combined bugs (5.72) rated harder. In the BugPilot study Claude Sonnet 4 solved 65.9% of SWE-smith tasks against 70.8% of SWE-bench Verified.

teach.title: How it works: the catch, then the mix

questions.q: What ratio of real to planted would you start with?
questions.a: No study I found gives one that transfers; SWE-Lego used about 18,000 real and 14,000 synthetic tasks. I'd train small runs at a few ratios and keep the best on held-out real bugs from unseen repos.

teach.title: How it works: the catch, then the mix

questions.q: How do you stop the agent learning a planted-bug shortcut?
questions.a: Remove the clue. In SWE-smith, issue texts that showed the failing test cut later reproduction attempts from 379 to 127 of 500 runs. My suggestions: write issues the way users do, add multi-file bugs such as BugPilot's feature-add bugs, and read rollouts that pass suspiciously fast.

teach.title: How it works: the catch, then the mix

questions.q: In reinforcement learning for a bug-fixing agent, what are the environment and the reward?
questions.a: The environment is a runnable copy of a repo with a bug, the issue text and the tests. The reward is the score for one attempt: 1 if the tests pass after the agent's fix, otherwise 0.

questions.q: How did real and synthetic bugs differ in the SWE-Lego dataset?
questions.a: Real tasks touched 3.7 files and 138.0 lines on average, synthetic ones 1.0 file and 18.8 lines. Logic slips were 29.9% of real bugs but 49.4% of synthetic ones.

teach.title: How it works: the catch, then the mix

questions.q: Which SWE-smith finding shows an environment teaching a shortcut?
questions.a: An agent trained on issue texts that showed the failing test later tried to reproduce the bug in only 127 of 500 SWE-bench Verified runs, against 379 for one trained on model-written issue texts.
